n: Enoch’s total life span on earth is given as 430 years. Combined with Moses 7:68, this means Zion existed for 365 of those years before being taken up.
Enoch’s son Methuselah was deliberately left on earth when Zion was taken, so God could keep His covenant that Noah would descend from Enoch.
Methuselah prophesies that all the world’s kingdoms will come from him through Noah — and takes pride in it. Even a prophet’s son can be tempted to claim glory that belongs to God.

f.g: took credit or pride for himself rather than giving glory to God.

n: A severe famine strikes, and many die. This disaster is a sign of the world’s spiritual decline before the Flood.
Methuselah becomes father of Lamech at 187. This genealogy matches Genesis 5 and traces the faithful line from Adam to Noah.

f.g: Not the murderer Lamech of Cain’s line (Moses 5:43-55), but a righteous descendant of Seth.

n: Methuselah lives another 782 years and has more children. The long lives of these patriarchs gave them centuries to teach the gospel to their descendants.
Methuselah dies at 969 — the longest life span recorded in the Bible, which made his name a byword for old age.
Lamech becomes a father at 182. The sentence continues in the next verse with the son’s name.
Lamech names his son Noah, hoping he will bring comfort and relief from the hard labor of farming cursed ground. The name sounds like the Hebrew words for rest and comfort.

f.g: Hebrew Noaḥ, related to nuaḥ “rest”; the verse plays on naḥam “comfort.”

f.w: the ground which the Lord hath cursed

n: Lamech lives 595 more years and has other children.
Lamech dies at 777. The faithful line from Adam to Noah is now complete.
Noah’s three sons are born — Japheth first, then Shem forty-two years later by the same mother, and Ham when Noah is 500. Genesis lists only Noah’s age at 500; this verse adds the birth order.
Noah and his sons listen to the Lord and are called “sons of God” — a title for those who make and keep covenants with Him, not heavenly beings.
As the population grows, the “sons of men” — those outside the covenant — marry Noah’s granddaughters simply because they are attractive, without regard to faith.

f.g: In Moses, people who reject God, in contrast to the covenant “sons of God.”

n: The Lord tells Noah that his granddaughters have “sold themselves” by marrying outside the covenant to men who refuse God. Marrying unbelievers drew Noah’s family toward the world.

f.g: gave themselves away cheaply, trading their covenant heritage for worldly attraction.

n: Noah becomes a prophet, teaching the same gospel that had been taught from the beginning with Adam.

f.w: even as it was in the beginning

n: The Lord warns that His Spirit will not always strive with people. He sets a 120-year window — many understand this as time left for repentance before the Flood.

f.g: to struggle with or plead with; the Spirit urges people toward good.

f.w: My Spirit shall not always strive with man

n: Violent “giants” try to kill Noah, but the Lord protects him and fills him with power. Like Enoch, Noah ministers under divine protection.

f.g: Hebrew nephilim (Genesis 6:4); probably powerful, violent men rather than literal monsters.

n: The Lord ordains Noah to the priesthood “after his own order” and sends him to preach the gospel, just as Enoch did. Latter-day Saints identify Noah with the angel Gabriel.

f.w: ordained Noah after his own order

n: Noah calls on everyone to repent, but they refuse to listen.

The people mock Noah, claiming to be “sons of God” themselves and boasting of normal life — eating, drinking, marrying, and raising mighty children. Jesus later cited these very days as a picture of the world before His return.

f.w: eating and drinking, and marrying and giving in marriage

n: God sees that wickedness has become universal — people are proud, and every thought in their hearts is evil all the time.

f.w: imagination of the thoughts of his heart

n: Despite rejection, Noah keeps preaching and pleading with the people to listen.

Noah’s message is the gospel of Jesus Christ itself: faith, repentance, baptism in Christ’s name, and the gift of the Holy Ghost — the same as later taught in the New Testament and Book of Mormon. Without it, the floods will come.

f.w: be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ

n: Noah is grieved to the heart that the Lord had ever made mankind, seeing what they have become. Genesis 6:6 says “it repented the Lord”; Joseph Smith’s inspired translation places this regret with Noah.

f.g: Noah regretted or was sorrowful; in Genesis 6:6 the KJV attributes this to the Lord.

n: The Lord declares He will destroy humanity and animals from the earth, because Noah is grieved and has prayed — and because the people are trying to kill Noah.
Noah finds grace — divine favor — because he is “just” and “perfect in his generation.” Perfect here means complete, whole, upright, not flawless. His sons also walk with God.
The earth is corrupt in God’s sight and full of violence. Violence is singled out as the defining sin of the pre-Flood world.
God looks and confirms the earth’s corruption: every living thing (“all flesh”) has corrupted its way.
God tells Noah that the end of all flesh has come because of violence, and announces the coming destruction. The story continues in Genesis 6:13 onward.

f.w: The end of all flesh is come before me
